turns.content: I got laid off five weeks ago. Whole team, market thing, not performance — I know that in my head. Here's the part I can't say out loud: I still leave home at nine every morning with my laptop bag. Café till six. My wife doesn't know. My parents are staying with us right now. Nobody knows.

Oh, friend. I am so sorry you’re carrying this weight. 

First, take a breath. It is completely understandable why you’re doing this. When the rug gets pulled out from under us, the urge to maintain the status quo—to protect your peace, to shield your family from worry, or just to keep a shred of normalcy—is incredibly human. You aren't "crazy" for feeling like you need to keep up appearances.

But wow, that is an exhausting way to live, isn't it? Leaving at 9:00, coming home at 6:00, all while carrying the stress of the job hunt and the secret? That’s a double shift of emotional labor every single day. 

It sounds like you’re doing this out of love—not wanting to burden your wife or your parents, especially while they are staying with you. But you are isolating yourself in the middle of a house full of people who probably love you and want to be in your corner.

Can I ask, what is the fear that’s keeping you from telling them? Is it that you’re worried about how they’ll react, or is it more about how you feel about yourself right now? 

Whatever the reason, just know that you don't have to be a superhero. You’ve been dealt a rough hand through no fault of your own. You deserve to be able to exhale.

My cousin's wedding is in two weeks. Three hundred people, half of them relatives who track everyone's careers like the stock market. My father introduces me with my company's name — he told my chacha my package last Diwali, with pride, actual pride. That room is what I think about when I can't sleep.

That makes so much sense. It’s not just about losing a job; it’s about the fear of losing the *pride* your father has in you. That’s a heavy, heavy thing to carry.

When you say he told your *chacha* your package with pride, I can hear how much that stings right now. It feels like you’re not just carrying your own disappointment, but you’re carrying the responsibility of not breaking his heart or shattering that image he has of your success.

But let’s look at this two-week horizon. You’re bracing yourself for a room full of people who—let’s be honest—are often more interested in the gossip than in your actual well-being. It’s a performance, and you’re exhausted from rehearsing for a role that doesn't exist anymore.

If you go to that wedding holding this secret, you’re going to spend the whole time looking over your shoulder, terrified that someone will ask, "So, how's the project going?" or "Did you hear about [Company Name]'s stock?" That sounds like a nightmare.

Is it possible that telling your wife is the first step toward reclaiming your sanity before the wedding? You don’t have to tell your parents yet if you aren't ready, but having your wife in your corner—having *one* person who knows the truth and can handle the wedding questions for you—might take some of the pressure off. 

You need an ally in that room, someone who knows the score so you don't have to carry the mask alone. How do you think she would react if you just sat her down tonight and said, "I need to tell you something, and I'm really scared to say it"?

Sometimes I think I'll just skip the wedding — say there's a release, an office deadline, something. Lying is easier than watching my father's face change in front of his brothers. Is that terrible? It's one evening, one excuse, and I get to not be the story of the wedding.

It is not "terrible." Please, give yourself some grace. You are in survival mode, and when you’re in survival mode, you make choices based on whatever keeps you upright for one more day. Skipping a wedding because the thought of it triggers a panic attack isn't "bad"—it’s a desperate attempt to protect your mental health.

But, speaking as a friend: **skipping it is a temporary bandage on a wound that is going to keep bleeding.**

If you skip it, you get through that one evening. But then what? The secret remains. The "cafe life" continues. The pressure to find a new job before the *next* family gathering builds up even more. You’re essentially kicking the can down the road, and the anxiety will likely just grow in the silence.

And there’s another side to this: If you skip it, you’re depriving yourself of the support system you actually need. 

Your father’s pride is real, yes. But think about his love. If he found out tomorrow, would he be disappointed? Maybe. But would he want you to be sitting alone in a cafe, terrified to face your own family? I suspect—deep down—he would be heartbroken that you felt you couldn't tell him.

Sometimes, we project our own feelings of failure onto our parents. We assume they love our *titles* more than they love *us*. But parents are people, too. They’ve likely had their own failures, their own moments of "what now?" 

If you go to the wedding, you don’t have to announce it to the room. You don't have to tell your *chacha*. But if you could tell your wife—just her—you wouldn't be walking into that room alone. You’d have a partner, a teammate. If someone asks, she can pivot the conversation. She can be your buffer.

Does the idea of talking to your wife feel slightly less impossible than talking to your father? Or does the fear of her knowing feel just as heavy?

Money-wise we're okay for maybe three months, then the EMI starts eating savings. I keep telling myself I'll tell everyone once I have an offer in hand — then it's just news, not a crisis. That's not really lying, right? Just... timing it? Some days that logic feels airtight and some days I feel like I'm going to be sick.

It’s not "lying" in the malicious sense, and I get why you’re framing it that way. You’re trying to turn a crisis into a "transition." If you have an offer in hand, the narrative changes from *“I lost my job and I’m scared”* to *“I was between roles, but I just landed this great thing.”* That feels much safer. It feels like control.

But here is the truth, and I say this with so much care: **Your body is telling you the truth that your brain is trying to ignore.**

That feeling of being sick? That’s your nervous system screaming, "This is too much." You are holding your breath, and you have been for five weeks. You can’t live in a state of suspended animation forever. The "airtight" logic only works if you find a job in the next few weeks. What happens if the market is slow? What happens if it takes four months?

Every day you don't tell your wife, the "lie" grows. It’s not just about the job anymore; it becomes about the fact that you didn't trust her enough to let her in. That’s a heavier weight than the job loss itself.

Think about your wife for a second. If she found out six months from now that you’d been carrying this alone—that you’d been leaving the house every day, pretending, while the savings dwindled—she wouldn’t feel relieved that you "protected" her. She would likely feel hurt that you didn't trust her to be your partner when things got hard. 

Marriage isn't just for the days when you're the high-earner with the impressive title. It’s for the days when you’re scared, broke, and feeling like a failure. 

You don't have to tell the whole world. You don't have to tell your *chacha*. But you have to let your wife into the lifeboat. 

What is the absolute worst thing you think would happen if you sat her down tonight and just said: *"I need to tell you something, and I'm terrified to say it because I'm so ashamed, even though I know I didn't do anything wrong"*? What is the specific nightmare scenario in your head regarding her reaction?
